title: A court that almost never executed (Mishnah Makkot 1:10)
hook: a court that executed once in seven years was called destructive; some said once in seventy

segments.voice: Yesterday, two hold a cloak: no witnesses, so each swears to half and they divide. Your line was each takes half. Did you find the piece that was really in dispute? Day one thousand eighty-four.

A court that puts someone to death once in seven years is called destructive. That, in plain English, is a sentence from the Mishnah, in the tractate Makkot. It isn't a slogan from outside the system. It comes from inside it, from the rabbis who taught the laws of the court. Then another voice: Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah says, once in seventy years. Then Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say: if we had sat on the court, no one would ever have been put to death. Today: a court that leans with its whole weight toward life.
screen: `ONCE IN SEVEN YEARS: DESTRUCTIVE.` → `SOME SAY SEVENTY.` → `WE WOULD NEVER HAVE EXECUTED.`

segments.voice: Sanhedrin. The Mishnah's name for the great court, and the name of the tractate that lays out how it works. The Torah does name crimes that carry death. The Mishnah keeps those laws, and then builds a court that leans hard the other way. Look at three of its rules. First, the order of speaking. In the tractate Sanhedrin, capital cases open with reasons to acquit, not reasons to convict. Anyone may argue for the accused. Second, the clock. A verdict of acquittal may be given the same day. A verdict of guilt has to wait until the next day, so the judges sleep on it. Third, the road. The Mishnah describes someone standing at the door of the court with a cloth in hand, and a rider posted at a distance. If anyone comes forward with something to say in the accused's favor, the cloth waves, the rider gallops off, and the procession stops. Even on the way out, the case can reopen. Then comes the argument in Makkot. Seven years. Seventy. Never. And the Mishnah doesn't let that last word stand alone. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel answers Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva: then you would multiply murderers in Israel. A court that never acts doesn't protect anyone either. The Mishnah leaves both voices on the page. Some readers take all this as a memory of how courts once ran; others read it as a picture of what a court ought to be. Either way, the weight is clear. When a life hangs in the balance, the system tilts toward keeping it.
screen: `ACQUITTAL IS ARGUED FIRST.` · `GUILT WAITS A NIGHT.` · `A CLOTH WAVES, A RIDER STOPS IT.` · `SEVEN, SEVENTY, NEVER, AND A WARNING.` · then, large: `LEAN TOWARD LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: lean toward mercy. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone you've been judging lately. A coworker, a relative, a stranger online. You don't have to change your mind. Just play the person at the court's door. Is there one thing to say in their favor? Something you don't know about their day. Something they did right. Find it, and let it be heard first, before the case against them. Then notice whether the verdict feels quite as finished. The bell holds the time.
Sanhedrin. The great court of the Mishnah, where the case for acquittal speaks first and a verdict of guilt waits a night. Today's word.
Your line: lean toward life. Today, when you catch yourself passing judgment on someone, let the argument in their favor go first. Day one thousand eighty-four.

howItsDone: Jews study the tractates Sanhedrin and Makkot as part of the Talmud's order of damages, and the debate in Makkot 1:10 is often cited in Jewish discussions of justice and the death penalty.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient court eager to punish.
what it means: a court built to lean toward life, with acquittal argued first, guilt delayed, and a way to stop even on the road.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:1 and 6:1, and the argument in Makkot 1:10: seven years, seventy, never, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's warning.
